correctness.rationale: Using the prior scalar maximum length gamma_gr(C_n)=n−2, the first closed neighborhood footprints three vertices and each of the n−3 following vertices footprints exactly one. The remaining undominated path has two distinct unselected dominated frontiers whenever its length≥2, allowing 2^(n−4) left/right words after v1. With one undominated vertex the legal last choice is that vertex or its two frontier neighbors, giving 3n2^(n−4) ordered maxima. The two unused vertices are an adjacent pair or distance-two pair. Dihedral transitivity yields 2^(n−3) sequences per adjacent omitted pair and 2^(n−4) per distance-two omitted pair for n≥5, with six sets and twelve sequences for n=4. Independent exhaustive search of actual legal sequences for n=4..9 recovered 12,30,72,168,384,864 maxima and set counts 6,10,12,14,16,18; arbitrary-n proof is frontier combinatorics.

originality.rationale: Brešar et al. supply the scalar cycle Grundy-domination number, and Brešar–Dravec study extremal-set uniqueness more generally. Neither inspected theorem gives the complete ordered sequence count, omitted-pair characterization, or multiplicities of each maximum set on an ordinary cycle. Resultary’s complete multipartite max-sequence census has a different graph family and does not dominate cycles. Possible older unindexed cycle combinatorics remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: Poorly indexed older enumerations of footprinting orders on cycles may exist.
Counts are ordinary Grundy closed-neighborhood maxima, not total, Z or L variants.

value.rationale: Counting all maximum ordered Grundy sequences and their underlying set orbits answers a natural stronger extremal enumeration question beyond a known scalar parameter. The two different per-set multiplicities reveal combinatorial structure and are directly reusable as cycle base cases for graph products.
